column1: /:id vs where: the two are different things. GET /users/:id and GET /tasks/:id look up one resource by its id and return 404 if it does not exist; only select applies to them (any other query parameter is ignored). where, sort, skip, limit and count apply to the collection endpoints (GET /users, GET /tasks), which always respond 200, with an empty list (or a count of 0) when nothing matches. An invalid JSON value in one of these parameters is a 400.
The API should be able to handle any combination of those parameters in a single request. For example, the following is a valid GET request:
javascript
http://localhost:3000/api/users?sort={"name": 1}&skip=60&limit=20
Here is the User Schema:
name - String
email - String
pendingTasks - [String] - The _id fields of the pending tasks that this user has
dateCreated - Date - should be set automatically by server
Here is the Task Schema:
name - String
description - String
deadline - Date
completed - Boolean
assignedUser - String - The _id field of the user this task is assigned to - default ""
assignedUserName - String - The name field of the user this task is assigned to - default "unassigned"
dateCreated - Date - should be set automatically by server to present date
We assume that each task can be assigned only to one user.
Requirements
Your database should be on MongoDB Atlas. NOTE: Please add "Allow access from anywhere" to your cluster in the IP Whitelist (This is usually not a good practice in real use.)

Responses from your API should be a JSON object with two fields. The first field should be named message and should contain a human readable String. The second field should be named data and should contain the actual JSON response object. For example, here is a valid response:
javascript
"message": "OK",
"data": {
"email": "khandek2@illinois.edu",
"name": "Sujay Khandekar"

Error responses from your API should also also be a JSON object with a message and data fields. Messages have to sensible and human readable so that on the client side it can be displayed to the user. Also, it should be independent of the server side technology that you are using. For example, your API should not return an error message directly from Mongoose to the client.

Your API should respond with appropriate HTTP status codes for both successful and error responses. You should at least have the following codes: 200 (success), 201 (created), 204(no content), 400(bad request), 404 (not found), 500 (server error).

You should implement the query string functionality by using the methods provided by Mongoose (as opposed to querying Mongoose for all the results and then doing the filtering/sorting/skipping etc. in your Node/Express application code).
Have server side validation for:
Users cannot be created (or updated) without a name or email. All other fields that the user did not specify should be set to reasonable values.
Multiple users with the same email cannot exist.
Tasks cannot be created (or updated) without a name or a deadline. All other fields that the user did not specify should be set to reasonable values.
Your API should guarantee two-way reference between Task and User, see Two-way references below.

Two-way references

A task is pending if it is not completed. Every pending task that is assigned to a user must be in that user's pendingTasks, and every id in a user's pendingTasks must be a pending task whose assignedUser/assignedUserName are that user's _id/name. An unassigned task has assignedUser: "" and assignedUserName: "unassigned". How you keep these in sync is up to you, but the following must hold after every request.

PUT /users/:id replaces the user with name, email and pendingTasks (missing pendingTasks means an empty list). dateCreated never changes. Let old be the user's previous pendingTasks and new the requested list:
Tasks
column2: What happens

column1: in old but not in new
column2: unassigned: assignedUser = "", assignedUserName = "unassigned"

column1: in new but not in old
column2: assigned to this user: assignedUser = <user _id>, assignedUserName = <user name>

column1: in new but currently assigned to another user
column2: the task moves: it is removed from the other user's pendingTasks, then assigned to this user as above

column1: already assigned to this user (completed ones too)
column2: stay assigned; if the user's name changed, their assignedUserName is updated

column1: PUT /tasks/:id replaces the task (missing fields get their defaults; dateCreated never changes):

If the task is assigned (assignedUser is set), it is added to that user's pendingTasks unless completed is true; a completed task is removed from the user's pendingTasks but stays assigned to the user.
If assignedUser changed, the task is removed from the previous user's pendingTasks.
Setting assignedUser to "" unassigns the task (assignedUserName becomes "unassigned").

assignedUser and assignedUserName must refer to the same user (400 otherwise; if assignedUserName is omitted you may fill it in). Changing assignedUser of an already completed task through PUT is allowed, since PUT replaces the whole task; the task is then simply assigned to the new user and is not added to anyone's pendingTasks.
Setting completed back to false on an assigned task makes it pending again (added to the user's pendingTasks).
POST /users with pendingTasks and POST /tasks with assignedUser follow the same rules as the corresponding PUT.

DELETE /tasks/:id removes the task from its assigned user's pendingTasks. DELETE /users/:id unassigns all of the user's tasks (including completed ones): assignedUser = "", assignedUserName = "unassigned".

Response format and status codes

Two-way references (27.5% of the grade, the hardest part)

PUT/POST user, PUT/POST task, and DELETE must all update the other side; see the "Two-way references" section of the README for the exact rules

A task moves from one user to another

Node.js and packages

Which Node.js version should I use? I get errors on Node 25. Answer: Use the current LTS release, Node 24 (nvm install --lts && nvm use --lts). The starter now uses current Mongoose (v9) and Express (v5), which work on Node 24 LTS; do not use odd-numbered, non-LTS releases such as Node 25. The old starter pinned Mongoose 5, which does not work on newer Node versions; if your package.json still says "mongoose": "^5...", update it (or re-copy it from the template) and run npm install. With Mongoose 9 you do not need options like useNewUrlParser/useUnifiedTopology, just mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGODB_URI), and callbacks are no longer supported (use async/await or promises).

Answer: Yes, it is allowed. PUT replaces the whole task and the new assignment must still be valid (existing user, matching assignedUserName). Because the task is completed it is not added to anyone's pendingTasks. A completed task keeps its assignedUser (that is how we know who completed it), so e.g. PUT with completed: true and the same assignedUser must succeed and remove the task from the user's pendingTasks. Not a website; it is a backend API. It has no pages and no buttons, and is only responsible for receiving requests, reading and writing the database, and then returning JSON data.
An analogy Building a todo app generally has three layers:
Frontend: the interface users see, such as the list, checkboxes and the "add task" button. This was not built this time.

Backend API: when the frontend's button is clicked, it sends a request here, for example "add a task for Alice". The backend validates the data, writes it to the database, and returns the result to the frontend. This is the layer built this time.
Database: where the data is actually stored. This time it is MongoDB Atlas.
What it can do specifically If you open https://mp3-al2o.onrender.com/api/tasks in a browser, you will see a string of JSON. It supports these operations:
Manage users: create, delete, update, read
Manage tasks: create, delete, update, read; a task has a name, a deadline, and whether it is completed

Assign tasks to users, with both sides' data automatically kept consistent. For example, marking a task completed automatically removes it from that user's "pending list"; deleting a user makes their tasks automatically "unassigned".
Queries: for example "only show completed tasks", "sort by name", "take only the first 20"

Why only the backend This course is Web Development, and MP3 specifically practices the backend, that is Node, Express and the database. A browser address bar can only send GET requests, so testing POST, PUT and DELETE generally uses a tool like Postman, and the autograder likewise sends requests automatically to test it.
If a later assignment asks you to write a frontend, the frontend's interface will call these endpoints to display and modify data.
